entries.text: Belle Ogden Armour, born in Ohio in the spring of 1843, was the widow of Philip D. Armour, the meat-packer whose stockyards and packing houses made Armour and Company one of the giants of Chicago. He died in 1901, and she stayed on in the big house at 2115 Prairie Avenue.

levels.8-10: Belle Ogden Armour was born in Ohio in the spring of 1843. Her husband was Philip D. Armour. He packed meat for a living. His stockyards and packing houses made his company one of the biggest in Chicago. He died in 1901. She stayed on in the big house at 2115 Prairie Avenue.

entries.text: The family lived here for nearly fifty years, and she died in the house in 1927. In the summer of 1904 she was sixty-one, with a ladies' maid, a parlor maid, a cook, a laundress, a valet and a coachman to keep the place running.

levels.8-10: The family lived here for almost fifty years. She died in the house in 1927. In the summer of 1904 she was sixty-one. Six workers helped run the house: two maids, a cook, a woman who did the wash, a man who helped with clothes and a driver for the horses.

entries.text: J. Ogden Armour, the meat-packer's son, lived here with his parents in the early 1890s. When his father died he took the head of Armour and Company, and by 1904 he had his own household elsewhere in the city.

levels.8-10: J. Ogden Armour was the son of the meat-packer. He lived here with his mom and dad in the early 1890s. When his father died, he took charge of the family company. By 1904 he had his own home in another part of the city.

entries.text: Thomas H. Bellas was born in Ireland in 1846 and came to America at thirty, in 1876. He made his money as a commission merchant in grain, the trade that filled Chicago's elevators, and settled his family at 1634 Prairie Avenue.

levels.8-10: Thomas H. Bellas was born in Ireland in 1846. He came to America in 1876, when he was thirty. He bought and sold grain for other people. Grain was a big business in Chicago, and it filled the city's tall grain buildings. He brought his family to 1634 Prairie Avenue.

entries.text: He was here with his wife, his three daughters and his brother-in-law in 1900. By the next spring the Blue Book listed Mrs. Bellas and her daughters without him.
